papers.title: SUDO: From Scientific Publications to Global Scholarly Discourse
papers.abstract: Scholarly Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) support literature search, scientific discovery, and agent-assisted research. Yet, most approaches to SKG construction pre-specify the knowledge unit to be represented, typically named scholarly entities or contribution-level statements, and retain only the publication content expressible through that unit. This choice produces two dominant yet distinct paradigms: concept-centric SKGs that preserve entities and local relations, and statement-centric SKGs that capture high-level discourse in sentences. In both cases, the graph reflects a chosen extraction target rather than how a paper constructs and communicates knowledge. We introduce SUDO, the Scholarly Upper Discourse Ontology, which defines how knowledge elements are organized and related to form a paper's research narrative, namely its scholarly discourse. Using linguistic principles that generalize across fields and tasks, SUDO enables each publication's scholarly discourse to be constructed from the bottom up as a coherent, source-grounded representation. Applied consistently across papers, the same structure connects their research narratives into a global scholarly discourse without discarding local context or provenance. We demonstrate SUDO's capabilities across a comprehensive suite of scholarly knowledge-modeling use cases and performance improvements on a downstream Large Language Model (LLM)-based scientific QA task.

papers.title: Is this Citation on Point?
papers.abstract: In 2023, a New York judge sanctioned two attorneys in \emph{Mata v. Avianca} for filing a brief containing hallucinated citations generated by ChatGPT. These failures can be largely caught by database lookups. The harder problem is detecting citations that point to real cases but do not support the propositions for which they are offered, a failure mode that existing evaluations of LLMs for legal use cases largely overlook. In this paper, we study proposition-level citation support verification through controlled perturbations of real legal citations obtained from two legal corpora. We either replace the cited case or change only the pinpoint page within the same case. Our evaluation of fourteen model configurations on the resulting examples shows that models catch $93$--$100\%$ of wrong-case corruptions, but they only catch $37$--$61\%$ of wrong-pinpoint corruptions on court opinions and $52$--$83\%$ on legal briefs. When models fail to catch wrong-pinpoint corruptions, they accept the citation based on topical overlap rather than page-level support. Larger-scale models and extended reasoning narrow the gap but do not close it: GPT-5.4 with high reasoning effort still misses $40\%$ of pinpoint mismatches on court opinions and $18\%$ on briefs. Prompting the model to verify support at the cited page improves recall, but it also raises the false positive rate. These results show that citation misrepresentations remain difficult to detect automatically. Recognizing the right legal topic and verifying support for the cited proposition are distinct capabilities, and current models conflate them.

papers.title: Sealed bets on emerging research topics: a protocol for judging early detection, applied to a detector and to eight research funders
papers.abstract: Tools that claim to detect emerging research topics are rarely judged on their own lists. Our main contribution is a protocol that makes such judgement possible. A bet freezes four things before its verdict can be known: the date of the photograph, the population of candidates, the verdict rule, and the comparison with chance drawn among the same candidates. The list has a fixed length, is read on two axes (champions and failures) against a computed ceiling, and is sealed by cryptographic fingerprint; sealing proves that a list existed at a date, not that it is right. A topic is a champion if its yearly volume of records triples within three years and reaches 100, a failure if it falls by 30%. We apply the protocol to one detector on PubMed/MEDLINE, in three separate blocks. On a retrospective benchmark (2017-2022), chance among the candidates yields 26.7 champions and 15.1 failures out of 120 slots; the detector yields 85 and 3, and under nine pre-registered variants of the verdict rule its champions stay between 2.5 and 5.0 times chance, with no more failures. The detector was developed with these verdicts known, and its specification is not published. Prospective validation rests on six sealed bets, judged in early 2029 and early 2030; only bets 5 and 6 test exactly the instrument of the benchmark. A secondary, exploratory study applies the same judge to eight research funders: under exact name matching, which may disadvantage grant texts, the detector's lists are more concentrated in future champions than the twenty topics named in the most grants of each funder (70.8% against 20.8% to 35.8%, chance 22.3%). We document data defects, negative results and the limits of each comparison.

papers.title: From Data Footprints to Researcher Fingerprints: Temporal Ego-centric Research Group Detection in Scientific Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Understanding who researchers collaborate with, when and how their research groups form, and how these evolve over time is a foundational prerequisite for constructing multidimensional, evidence-based researcher fingerprints -- a requirement that has become increasingly urgent in the context of ongoing reforms in research evaluation advocated by initiatives such as DORA, the Leiden Manifesto, and CoARA. In this paper, we propose an egocentric approach for fine-grained research group detection, operating at the scale of individual researchers' ego networks, as extracted from Scientific Knowledge Graphs (SKGs), and requiring the ego node to be present in all identified research groups -- a constraint that is not merely technical but reflects a commitment to researcher-centred analysis. Our approach builds on the Leiden algorithm as its computational core and is grounded in SKGs, which provide the heterogeneous, open scholarly metadata necessary to trace collaboration patterns at scale in a reproducible and transparent manner. We evaluate the proposed method through a user evaluation involving 10 researchers with diverse backgrounds and career stages, demonstrating its ability to surface meaningful and interpretable collaboration structures. The research groups identified constitute the structural scaffold upon which richer characterisations of scholarly identity -- including roles, seniority, contribution types, and publication patterns -- can be built in subsequent work, contributing to the broader goal of fairer and more transparent research assessment.

papers.title: Officially corrected errors persist in AI training data: preregistered measurements on EU law, Internet standards and retracted science
papers.abstract: Official texts are corrected after publication: EU corrigenda, verified RFC errata, retractions. We measured whether these corrections are present in four public datasets used to train language models, and what models answer about the corrected passages. In EurlexResources, a legal training dataset, 1,989 of 2,082 testable single-language corrections to EU acts (95.5%, 94.6-96.3) remain in their erroneous form; in a random sample of 100, 46 change the meaning, a figure, a cross-reference, the competent authority or the scope (20 without scope). At least 124 corrected EU-law errors and at least 60 verified RFC errata (38 classified "Technical") are reproduced in their erroneous form in FineWeb-2 and in a sample of FineWeb. About 12,200 retracted papers (11,700-12,500) are present in the peS2o corpus, 79% with no mention of the retraction; separately, 53% of a random sample of retracted papers are still cited at least a year after retraction (OpenAlex). Asked 59 questions on serious corrected errors without documents, five models gave the erroneous version in 45% of the answers in which they committed to one version (31-60% allowing for clustering by question): 53% for scope corrections, 32% for the others. One answer in 295 said it did not know. Shown both versions side by side, the models chose the corrected one in 53% of cases (49-57), and naming the act made no difference; when each version carried its date and the corrigendum label, the four larger models chose it in 99-100% of cases. A comparison between a legal masked language model and its base model is null, against our bet: we do not show that model answers come from the datasets measured. All steps were preregistered and their fingerprints timestamped in the Bitcoin blockchain; six controls failed, several bets were lost, and every deviation is reported. Data and proofs: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23642239.

papers.title: Interpreting LLM Scores in Peer Review: Alignment and Divergence Across Prompts, Domains, and Manuscript Features
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) scores are being studied as information for scholarly evaluation. Interpreting these scores requires evidence about agreement with human judgments and its variation across evaluation conditions. Guided by an argument-based approach to validation, we compare four LLMs on 7,083 public ICLR 2024 submissions under a standard review condition and examine ten prompt conditions using DeepSeek-V3.2. We distinguish average score divergence, paper-level absolute error, and rank correlation, then examine domain differences and adjusted manuscript-feature associations. For DeepSeek-V3.2, Area Chair guidance reduces mean rating divergence from 1.460 to 0.199 points and mean absolute error from 1.577 to 0.942, while rank correlation changes from 0.377 to 0.387. Historical references combined with downward scoring instructions yield mean divergence of 0.052 and rank correlation of 0.321. Domain differences remain after global calibration. Longer titles have positive adjusted associations with rating divergence, and formula density has negative associations across all four configurations. These findings connect score interpretation to the scoring procedure, evaluation context, and manuscript information represented in the comparison. They show why aggregate alignment, manuscript ordering, and correspondence within manuscript groups require distinct evidence when evaluating LLM-generated scholarly assessment information.

papers.title: The Hidden Costs of Gatekeeping in Open Science: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from arXiv's Endorsement Policy Tightening
papers.abstract: Preprint servers and open science platforms have become core infrastructure through which scientific knowledge circulates on the Web, greatly facilitating the dissemination and diffusion of online scientific information. Yet to safeguard content quality, many of these platforms rely on existing members to vouch for newcomers; how such network-mediated gatekeeping reshapes entry barriers across different scientific communities remains systematically underexplored. To address this, I examine the potential unequal impacts of this mechanism through arXiv's tightening of its endorsement policy in early 2026. Using the metadata of three million arXiv papers and the co-authorship networks of each research community, I compare the influx and dynamics of first-time submitters before and after the policy across eight disciplines. The findings show that the policy reduced the entry of new authors, and this reduction was concentrated in fields where co-authorship ties are sparse, while fields with dense collaboration networks were largely spared. A comparison with a parallel preprint server in biology suggests that this likely reflects a shift in where researchers choose to post rather than a decline in research activity. These findings demonstrate that the network structure of a scientific community shapes who can enter online scientific production, advancing our understanding of how the Web's open knowledge infrastructure shapes inequality in the diffusion of science.

papers.title: Is the arXiv Apocalypse upon us? A break in preprint growth coincident with agentic AI
papers.abstract: As an experiment in agentic assisted analysis, we used an agentic AI model to analyse the effect of agentic AI on arXiv submissions; data acquisition, analysis and the first draft were carried out by the model under the author's direction. Monthly arXiv submissions have grown exponentially for three decades, at about $9\%$ per year. Fitting a piecewise log-linear trend with seasonal modulation to the full record, we find two post-pandemic breaks in growth rate. The first, in mid-2022, precedes ChatGPT and is carried by the expansion of AI research within computer science (CS); outside CS, growth from 2022 to 2025 remained at $8\%$ per year. The second, between December 2025 and February 2026, follows the release of models capable of extended autonomous work and is absent from the AI categories themselves. Since December 2025 submissions without a CS listing have run $17\%$ above trend, and in September 2026 total submissions reached a record $40\,363$. The excess is largest in mathematics, where submissions doubled within a year, and follows a gradient from formal and theoretical fields to experimental ones that is not ordered by surveyed rates of AI-tool adoption. In mathematics the increase is distributed across subfields and authors, two-thirds of it arising from a larger number of distinct authors rather than from a few prolific submitters. Across fields the clearest signature is a shift to single authorship: solo-authored papers rose by $70\%$ within a year in mathematics and condensed matter, and by $44\%$ in quantitative biology even as its total output fell, but not in experimental particle physics. The analysis is deliberately agnostic of LLM-detection methods: it uses only submission counts and metadata, with treatment timing fixed by calendar dates, and is therefore free of the outcome-triggered timing bias of author-level studies.
